Fix a field $k$ and use algebraic tensor products over $k$ as in [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. A **coalgebra** is a $k$-vector space $C$ with $k$-linear maps
$$
\Delta:C\longrightarrow C\otimes C,\qquad \varepsilon:C\longrightarrow k
$$
such that
$$
\alpha_{C,C,C}\circ(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}_C)\circ\Delta
=(\mathrm{id}_C\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta
$$
and
$$
\lambda_C\circ(\varepsilon\otimes\mathrm{id}_C)\circ\Delta
=\mathrm{id}_C
=\rho_C\circ(\mathrm{id}_C\otimes\varepsilon)\circ\Delta.
$$
Here $\alpha$ is the tensor associator and $\lambda_C,\rho_C$ are the tensor unit isomorphisms. They are the maps supplied by [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] and [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. Thus the coassociativity equation has common target $C\otimes(C\otimes C)$; no unmentioned equality of differently parenthesized tensor spaces is assumed. The tensor products are algebraic, so each tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors.

derivations.claim: The map $C\otimes D\to(C\otimes D)\otimes(C\otimes D)$ is the composite of the tensor maps induced by $\Delta_C,\Delta_D$ and the middle-factor flip from [F2]–[F3]; the counit map is $\varepsilon_C\otimes\varepsilon_D$ followed by the unit isomorphism [F4]. Thus both formulas are well-defined linear maps, and on any elementary tensor they have the stated values.

On $c\otimes d$, either iterated coproduct first applies the corresponding threefold coproducts to $c$ and $d$ and then interleaves their factors in the order $C,D,C,D,C,D$. Coassociativity of $\Delta_C$ and $\Delta_D$ from [F5] makes these threefold coproducts equal for the two parenthesizations, and the coherent associators and flips in [F3] give the same interleaving; therefore $(\Delta_{C\otimes D}\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta_{C\otimes D}=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta_{C\otimes D})\Delta_{C\otimes D}$ on elementary tensors.

Applying the left counit to the displayed coproduct gives $\sum\varepsilon_C(c_{(1)})\varepsilon_D(d_{(1)})(c_{(2)}\otimes d_{(2)})=c\otimes d$ by the two left counit equations in [F5]; applying the right counit gives $\sum\varepsilon_C(c_{(2)})\varepsilon_D(d_{(2)})(c_{(1)}\otimes d_{(1)})=c\otimes d$ by the two right counit equations.

Both sides of every identity in steps 1.2–1.3 are linear maps, and elementary tensors span each tensor product by [F1]. The identities therefore hold on all of their domains, proving that the stated maps make $C\otimes D$ a coalgebra.

derivations.claim: The stated maps make $k$ a coalgebra: for $r\in k$, both iterated coproducts of $\Delta_k(r)=r(1\otimes1)$ equal $r(1\otimes1\otimes1)$ under the coherent associator [F7], and either counit contraction equals $r$ under the unit isomorphism [F6]. The induced tensor maps are well-defined by [F8].

The maps in condition 1 are unital algebra homomorphisms exactly when they preserve products and units, as required in the bialgebra definition [F3]. With the tensor-product algebra [F5], these requirements are precisely $\Delta(ab)=\Delta(a)\Delta(b)$, $\Delta(1)=1\otimes1$, $\varepsilon(ab)=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)$, and $\varepsilon(1)=1$.

The comultiplication equation for $m$ to be a coalgebra map [F1], evaluated on $a\otimes b$, is $\Delta(m(a\otimes b))=(m\otimes m)\Delta_{H\otimes H}(a\otimes b)=\sum a_{(1)}b_{(1)}\otimes a_{(2)}b_{(2)}$. By [F4]–[F5], this is exactly $\Delta(ab)=\Delta(a)\Delta(b)$. Both sides are linear in $a\otimes b$ and elementary tensors span $H\otimes H$ by [F2], while $m\otimes m$ is well-defined by [F8]. Thus the map equation holds exactly when that multiplicativity equation holds for all $a,b$.

The counit equation for $m$ to be a coalgebra map [F1] is $\varepsilon(m(a\otimes b))=\varepsilon_{H\otimes H}(a\otimes b)$, which by [F4] is $\varepsilon(ab)=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)$. Since elementary tensors span [F2], equality on all of them is equivalent to equality of the linear maps.

For $u:k\to H$, the coalgebra-map equations [F1] at $\lambda\in k$ are $\Delta(u(\lambda))=(u\otimes u)\Delta_k(\lambda)$ and $\varepsilon(u(\lambda))=\varepsilon_k(\lambda)$. By linearity and the formulas in the Statement, these become $\lambda\Delta(1)=\lambda(1\otimes1)$ and $\lambda\varepsilon(1)=\lambda$, using the source coalgebra established in step 1.1. They hold for every $\lambda$ exactly when $\Delta(1)=1\otimes1$ and $\varepsilon(1)=1$. Steps 1.3–1.4 show that $m$ is a coalgebra map exactly when the two product equations hold; the two unit equations supply the remaining equations in step 1.2. Therefore condition 2 holds exactly when condition 1 holds.

Give $\operatorname{Hom}_k(H\otimes H,H)$ convolution using the coalgebra of [F2] and the algebra of $H$. The maps $\phi=S\circ m$ and $\psi(a\otimes b)=S(b)S(a)$ are both two-sided inverses of $m$: $(\phi*m)(a\otimes b)=\sum S(a_{(1)}b_{(1)})a_{(2)}b_{(2)}=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)1$ and $(m*\phi)(a\otimes b)=\sum a_{(1)}b_{(1)}S(a_{(2)}b_{(2)})=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)1$ by the antipode equations at $ab$, multiplicativity of $\Delta$, and multiplicativity of $\varepsilon$; also $(\psi*m)(a\otimes b)=\sum S(b_{(1)})S(a_{(1)})a_{(2)}b_{(2)}=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)1$ and $(m*\psi)(a\otimes b)=\sum a_{(1)}b_{(1)}S(b_{(2)})S(a_{(2)})=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)1$ by first contracting $S(a_{(1)})a_{(2)}$ or $b_{(1)}S(b_{(2)})$ and then the remaining antipode pair. The right side is the convolution unit on $H\otimes H$ by [F2].

Give $\operatorname{Hom}_k(H,H\otimes H)$ convolution using $\Delta$ on the source and the tensor-product algebra on the target. The map $\Phi=\Delta\circ S$ is a two-sided inverse of $\Delta$: $(\Phi*\Delta)(h)=\sum\Delta(S(h_{(1)}))\Delta(h_{(2)})=\Delta(\sum S(h_{(1)})h_{(2)})=\varepsilon(h)(1\otimes1)$ and $(\Delta*\Phi)(h)=\sum\Delta(h_{(1)})\Delta(S(h_{(2)}))=\Delta(\sum h_{(1)}S(h_{(2)}))=\varepsilon(h)(1\otimes1)$ by multiplicativity of $\Delta$ and the two antipode equations. Since $\varepsilon$ is an algebra map, applying it to $\sum S(h_{(1)})h_{(2)}=\varepsilon(h)1$ gives $(\varepsilon\circ S)*\varepsilon=\varepsilon$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_k(H,k)$. derivations.claim: By [F1], $kG$ is the free vector space with basis $G$. The group product on basis elements extends to the bilinear pairing $(\sum a_g g,\sum b_hh)\mapsto\sum a_gb_h(gh)$, with finite output support; [F9] gives its multiplication map on $kG\otimes kG$. Associativity follows on basis triples from $(gh)r=g(hr)$ and then on all finite sums by bilinearity, while $e$ is a two-sided unit. Define $\Delta$ and $\varepsilon$ by their displayed values on this basis and extend linearly.

By [F2] and [F4], the assignments $x\mapsto x\otimes1+1\otimes x$ and $x\mapsto0$ extend uniquely to algebra maps $\Delta:k[x]\to k[x]\otimes k[x]$ and $\varepsilon:k[x]\to k$. The induced maps $\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}$ and $\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta$ are algebra maps by [F4], [F8], with their codomains identified by the coherent associators [F7]. Both iterated coproduct maps send $x$ to $x\otimes1\otimes1+1\otimes x\otimes1+1\otimes1\otimes x$ and send $1$ to $1$, so they agree by the universal property [F2]; likewise each counit composite and $\mathrm{id}_{k[x]}$ agree on $x$ and $1$. Thus $k[x]$ is a bialgebra.

Suppose now that $G$ is finite. The point masses $\delta_g$ form a basis of $k^G$, and [F3] identifies the basis $\delta_x\otimes\delta_y$ with the point-mass basis of $k^{G\times G}$. Thus the formula $\Delta(f)(x,y)=f(xy)$ defines a linear map into $k^G\otimes k^G$. On $(x,y,z)\in G^3$, the two iterated coproducts evaluate to $f((xy)z)$ and $f(x(yz))$, which agree by associativity in $G$, with the two parenthesizations identified by [F7]; the left and right counit composites evaluate to $f(ex)$ and $f(xe)$, both $f(x)$. Pointwise multiplication and evaluation at $e$ make $k^G$ a unital algebra, and $\Delta$ and $\varepsilon$ preserve products and units pointwise, so the bialgebra compatibility holds.

Write $x_g$ for the generator indexed by $g$ in the free associative algebra $k\langle G\rangle$ and let $E=\{1-x_e\}\cup\{x_gx_h-x_{gh}:g,h\in G\}$, where $gh$ in the subscript is the group product. Set $Q:=k\langle G\rangle/(E)$. The assignment $x_g\mapsto g$ extends to an algebra map $k\langle G\rangle\to kG$ by [F10]; it kills $E$ because $e$ is the unit and the multiplication in step 1.1 extends the group law. By [F11] it descends to $\bar\phi:Q\to kG$. Define $\psi:kG\to Q$ linearly by $\psi(g)=[x_g]$. It is unital since $[x_e]=1_Q$, and it preserves basis products because $[x_g][x_h]=[x_{gh}]=\psi(gh)$ by the relations; bilinearity makes it an algebra map. The composite $\bar\phi\psi$ fixes every basis vector of $kG$, so it is the identity. The maps $\psi\bar\phi$ and $\mathrm{id}_Q$ agree on the generator classes $[x_g]$; uniqueness in [F10]–[F11] gives their equality. Thus the quotient presentation descends to the explicitly constructed group algebra of step 1.1.

Define $S(x^n)=(-1)^n x^n$ linearly. Since the two summands $x\otimes1$ and $1\otimes x$ commute, the binomial theorem gives $\Delta(x^n)=\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj x^j\otimes x^{n-j}$. Hence both antipode products on $x^n$ equal $x^n\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj(-1)^j=(1-1)^n x^n$, which is $1$ for $n=0$ and $0$ for $n>0$; these are exactly $u\varepsilon(x^n)$. Monomials form a basis, so linearity proves both equations for every polynomial, in every characteristic. This proves the Hopf assertion by [F6].

Define $S(f)(x)=f(x^{-1})$. Evaluating the two antipode products at $x\in G$ gives $\Delta(f)(x^{-1},x)=f(e)$ and $\Delta(f)(x,x^{-1})=f(e)$: evaluation after $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})$ or $m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)$ is respectively evaluation of the function on $G\times G$ at $(x^{-1},x)$ or $(x,x^{-1})$.
